name: Abau
confidence_why: Lock's 2011 reference grammar and his 2007 phonology both state that primary stress always falls on the first syllable of the word, Laycock 1965 (as reported in Lock 2011) said the same except for words with a schwa that Lock reanalyses as /o/, and Bailey 1975's older claim that Abau has two register tonemes was checked pair by pair and rejected by Lock 2007 and had already been doubted by Laycock and Z'graggen 1975, so the record rests on one modern fieldworker's analysis with older support and no live objection.

catalog_locator: Lock 2011 sec. 2.3 'Tone, stress and syllables', p.20; sec. 2.5 'Word boundaries and stress', pp.22-23; sec. 4.2.1 pp.126-127; sec. 7.5.2 pp.277-278. Lock 2007 sec. 2.4.6 pp.21-22, sec. 5.1 p.41. OPD 'Suprasegmentals' p.2-3.
catalog_quote: [Lock 2011:20] The stress in Abau always occurs word initially. Bailey never commented on stress. Laycock (1965b) states that stress occurs word initially, or occurs on the second syllable when the word contains /ə/. As stated before, the current analysis does not have this central vowel. Six of the seven examples with /ə/ mentioned by Laycock (1965b:117) are analysed currently as /o/. These words have the stress on the first syllable (e.g. hohkwe ‘the two of them’). [Lock 2011:22] The phonological word is defined as a unit with one primary stress. In Abau, primary stress is associated with the first syllable of the phonological word. The syllable with primary stress is assigned higher pitch and intensity than the other syllables. The lowest pitch occurs on the last syllable. [Lock 2011:23] The distribution of the primary stress is used as a criterion for marking word boundaries. The following rule can be formulated: A pitch-carrying unit should be analysed as the onset of a new word, whenever this unit carries a higher pitch than its preceding unit. [Lock 2007:21-22] We have found stress to always occur word initially. Stress is not only realised by loudness but especially by the accompanying highest pitch within the word ... Words with three or more syllables have a predictable stress and pitch pattern; the first syllable will be most salient in terms of loudness and pitch, while each syllable following will be lower in pitch and volume than the preceding syllable.

'These words have the stress on the first syllable (e.g. hohkwe 'the two of them').'); the compiler ellipsis elides only the sentence 'Six of the seven examples with /ə/ mentioned by Laycock (1965b:117) are analysed currently as /o/.' p.36 = printed p.22, sec…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the first syllable of the phonological word, realised as the highest pitch and greatest intensity in the word, with pitch falling steadily to the last syllable; a rise in pitch relative to the preceding syllable diagnoses the onset of a new word. No lexical tone (Bailey's 1975 tone claim rejected).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as a regular system; pitch/intensity simply decline syllable by syllable after the initial peak. Lock 2007:22 notes a secondary peak on the third syllable of linker-reduplications (lowp-a-lowp 'all') and a noun following a modifying interrogative 'has secondary stress' (2011:278).
new_statements.exceptions: Verbal manner/direction prefixes take the primary stress away from the head verb's first syllable (stress remains word-initial on the prefixed word, 2011:126-127); compound nouns form one stress unit with primary stress on the first component and a larger pitch drop on the second (2007:22; 2011:277-278); interrogative+noun NPs form one stress unit with initial stress on the interrogative; reduplications with a linker (lowp-a-lowp) have a secondary rise on the third syllable; phrase-final markers never carry prominent stress. Laycock 1965 reported second-syllable stress in schwa words, which Lock reanalyses as initial-stressed /o/ words.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (defined by one primary stress); Lock also describes phrase stress (on the head of each phrase) and sentence stress peaking on the clause-final verb (2007:41-42; 2011 sec. 2.5). Statements based mainly on the Central dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Lock's description is of Abau as a whole (glottocode abau1245), based primarily on the Central dialect (Yabru area) with notes on Up-River and Down-River dialect differences; no separate glottocodes needed. The OPD sheet labels the language 'Abau (Green River)'.

tone_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1997. Tone systems in New Guinea. Linguistic Typology 1(3): 347-386. doi:10.1515/lity.1997.1.3.347
tone_statements.quote: Abau is one of the few languages reported to be in the Sepik phylum that uses tone in its phonological system (Bailey 1975). ... Finally, Bailey (1975: 58) concludes that 'tone [is] phonemic and obviously carries a considerable functional load'. ... [T]hese data show us that we have a contrast on monosyllables between [H] and L, and on disyllables between HH, HL and LL.
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Abau is presented as a syllable-tone language (H/L per syllable, with sandhi before certain particles) on the strength of Bailey 1975. The entry follows Lock 2007/2011, which found no lexical tone and rejects Bailey, so the article's classification conflicts with the entry.

readall_conflicts: Bailey 1975 (the excerpt read here, pp.32-38) treats Abau as a register-tone language with two tonemes, lexemic tone on nouns and grammemic tone on verbs, and makes no stress statement at all; this conflicts in type with the catalog's fixed word-initial stress from Lock 2011/2007/1997. The conflict is resolved in the later literature, not merely asserted: Lock 2007:21-22 and 2011:20 reanalyse every tonal minimal pair Bailey listed as an incorrect interpretation and find no tone, and Laycock and Z'graggen 1975:744-5 (per Lock 2011:20) had already questioned Bailey's tonal claim because Laycock 1965b said Abau is not tonal. Laycock 1965 could not be opened; per Lock 2011:20 it places stress word-initially except on the second syllable of words containing /ə/, a vowel Lock's analysis does not have (those words are reanalysed as /o/ or /ow/ with initial stress), so any residual disagreement is about the vowel inventory rather than the stress rule.

sources.citation: Lock, Arjen. 2007. Phonology Essentials, Abau Language. Ukarumpa: SIL International (March 2007). 70 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 2.4.6 pp.21-22: 'We have found stress to always occur word initially', realised by loudness and highest pitch; words of 3+ syllables have descending pitch/volume after the first; reduplicated words with a linker (lowp-a-lowp) and compound nouns are exceptions to the normal contour (third syllable/second component gets a secondary peak or a larger pitch drop). Sec. 5.1 p.41: 'Stress in Abau occurs word initially'; phrase stress on head of phrase, sentence peak on the clause-final verb. No lexical tone (contra Bailey 1975).
